To address GPU memory constraints, particularly with large models and input sequences, OpenFold implements **chunking** and **activation checkpointing**. Chunking, facilitated by utilities like [`chunk_layer`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py#L213) from [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py), involves breaking down large tensor operations into smaller, manageable segments. This allows computations to proceed without exhausting GPU memory, as intermediate activations can be discarded after use and recomputed later if needed. For instance, in the [`OuterProductMean`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/outer_product_mean.py#L27) module, chunking ensures that the outer product calculation for large MSAs remains memory-efficient ([`_chunk`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/msa.py#L92) method in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/outer_product_mean.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/outer_product_mean.py)). Similarly, various attention mechanisms ([`MSAAttention`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/msa.py#L38) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/msa.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/msa.py), [`TriangleAttention`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/triangular_attention.py#L32) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/triangular_attention.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/triangular_attention.py)) also utilize chunking.

**Activation checkpointing**, controlled by parameters like [`checkpoint_blocks`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/checkpointing.py#L43) in [`EvoformerStack`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py#L769) ([`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py)), further reduces memory footprint during training. This technique avoids storing all intermediate activations in memory by recomputing them during the backward pass. This is especially beneficial for deep architectures like the Evoformer. The [`EvoformerStack`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py#L769) and [`ExtraMSAStack`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py#L1067) use this extensively.

OpenFold also supports **memory offloading** where tensors are temporarily moved from GPU to CPU memory during inference, particularly when processing large models. This is managed by the [`_offload_inference`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/model.py#L461) methods found in modules such as [`EvoformerBlock`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py#L387) and [`StructureModule`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/structure_module.py#L817) ([`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py), [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/structure_module.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/structure_module.py)) and the [`embed_templates_offload`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/template.py#L490) function within the template processing ([`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/template.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/template.py)). This allows processing of larger protein systems than would otherwise fit on a single GPU.

**Optimized Attention Kernels**
The model integrates various high-performance attention kernels to speed up computations, especially within the Evoformer blocks. The [`Attention`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py#L360) primitive defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py) serves as a configurable wrapper for these optimized implementations. This includes:

*   **DeepSpeed Evoformer Attention**: Leveraging DeepSpeed's specialized kernel ([`DS4Sci_EvoformerAttention`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/docs/source/index.md#L53)) for Evoformer operations, which can provide significant speedups.
*   **FlashAttention**: Utilizing the [`flash_attn`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/config.py#L61) library for faster attention computations, particularly beneficial for sequences where the quadratic complexity of attention becomes a bottleneck.
*   **cuEquivariance Attention**: Integration of [`triangle_attention`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/docs/source/Inference.md#L170) from the [`cuequivariance_torch`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/config.py#L74) library, used in modules like [`TriangleAttention`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/triangular_attention.py#L32) ([`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/triangular_attention.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/triangular_attention.py)), which offers optimized triangular attention calculations.
*   **Low-Memory Attention (LMA)**: A custom implementation ([`_lma`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py#L758)) that chunks query and key/value tensors to perform attention iteratively, reducing memory consumption for very long sequences at the cost of some computational overhead.

The choice between these kernels is often governed by configuration flags and their availability in the environment, allowing OpenFold to adapt to different hardware setups and performance requirements.

**Mixed-Precision Training**
While not explicitly detailed as a module, the handling of [`bfloat16`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/build_deepspeed_config.py#L275) precision in modules like [`Linear`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py#L138) and [`LayerNorm`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py#L229) ([`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py)) and the use of [`torch.cuda.amp.autocast`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/heads.py#L164) in [`OuterProductMean`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/outer_product_mean.py#L27) ([`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/outer_product_mean.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/outer_product_mean.py)) indicate support for mixed-precision training. This technique combines [`fp16`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/build_deepspeed_config.py#L271) (or [`bfloat16`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/build_deepspeed_config.py#L275)) with [`fp32`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/docs/source/Inference.md#L149) operations to reduce memory usage and increase computational speed on compatible hardware, without significant loss of numerical stability.

**TorchScript Optimization**
OpenFold utilizes TorchScript to optimize model performance by selectively scripting or tracing parts of the neural network. The utilities in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/torchscript.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/torchscript.py) allow for [`torch.jit.script`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py#L286) or [`torch.jit.trace`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/trace_utils.py#L143) to be applied to specific submodules, such as [`Attention`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py#L360) and [`EvoformerBlock`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/evoformer.py#L387). This can lead to faster execution by allowing PyTorch to optimize and serialize computation graphs, and to potentially export models for deployment in environments where Python runtime is not available.

## Protein Structure Representation and Numerical Operations
Protein structure data within OpenFold is managed through a set of utilities designed for parsing, converting, and representing protein structural information, as detailed in the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np) directory. This includes core functionality for refining protein coordinates through Amber energy minimization and a centralized system for amino acid properties.

The [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) dataclass, defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py), standardizes protein structure representation. This dataclass encapsulates atom positions, amino acid types, masks, residue indices, and B-factors. It provides functionalities for converting between various protein data formats, such as PDB and ModelCIF strings, and for constructing [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) objects from model predictions. For instance, [`from_pdb_string`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L89) parses PDB strings, while [`to_pdb`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L321) and [`to_modelcif`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L446) convert [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) objects back into PDB or ModelCIF formats.

Post-prediction refinement of protein structures is handled by the Amber energy minimization process, which uses OpenMM to improve physical realism and reduce steric clashes. This functionality is primarily implemented in the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax) directory. The [`AmberRelaxation`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/relax.py#L23) class in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/relax.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/relax.py) orchestrates iterative, restrained Amber energy minimization, configurable with parameters such as maximum iterations, tolerance, and GPU usage. The underlying minimization process, managed by [`run_pipeline`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/amber_minimize.py#L475) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/amber_minimize.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/amber_minimize.py), involves cleaning the protein, applying harmonic positional restraints, running OpenMM's energy minimization, and iteratively refining the structure based on detected violations. Structural violations are identified using functions like [`get_violation_metrics`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/amber_minimize.py#L399), which help guide the relaxation by adjusting restraints. PDB cleanup utilities, found in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/cleanup.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/cleanup.py), leverage [`pdbfixer`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/environment.yml#L14) to address common PDB issues, such as nonstandard residues and missing atoms, and also include custom fixes for specific structural anomalies. Utility functions in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/relax/utils.py) support these operations by overwriting PDB coordinates and B-factors, and validating atom types.

Amino acid properties, atomic structures, and bond geometry constants are centralized in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/residue_constants.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/residue_constants.py). This file stores data for all standard amino acid types and provides utility functions for converting sequences to one-hot encodings and for managing rigid group transformations. It precomputes mappings and relative positions for atoms within different rigid groups of each residue type, which are crucial for geometric calculations. It also defines methods to compute lower and upper bounds for inter-atomic distances, essential for assessing steric clashes and bond length violations.

Fundamental mathematical and computational utilities for handling 3D geometric operations, rotations, and rigid body transformations are provided within the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry) directory. This module offers core data structures such as [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25) for 3D vectors, [`Rot3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py#L30) for rotation matrices, and [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30) for rigid transformations, enabling operations like composition, inversion, and point application. The [`QuatRigid`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py#L10) module in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py) translates neural network activations into [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30) transformations using quaternion representations for rotation, providing a differentiable interface between model outputs and geometric transformations. This allows for seamless integration of predicted values into structural representations. For further details on these core geometric data structures, refer to [Core 3D Geometric Data Structures and Operations](#protein-structure-representation-and-numerical-operations-core-3d-geometric-data-structures-and-operations).

### Protein Data Representation and Conversion
Protein structure data is standardized and managed through the [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) dataclass defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py). This dataclass stores key structural attributes, including atom positions, amino acid types, atom masks, residue indices, B-factors, and chain indices.

The system provides functionalities to convert between the [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) dataclass and various standard protein data formats. It can parse PDB strings into [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) objects and generate PDB strings from [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) objects, including handling chain termination records and PDB headers. Similarly, it supports conversion from ProteinNet formatted strings, extracting sequence, tertiary coordinates, and masking information. For ModelCIF format, [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) objects can be transformed into ModelCIF strings, incorporating detailed system, entity, asymmetric unit, and assembly information, along with quality metrics derived from B-factors.

Additionally, the system includes utilities for generating ideal atom masks based on standard heavy atoms for each amino acid type and for constructing [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) objects directly from model prediction outputs, including the assignment of chain indices and B-factors. The [`Protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) dataclass includes validation to ensure the number of unique chain indices does not exceed the PDB format limit. For a comprehensive overview of protein structure refinement, see [Protein Structure Refinement and Relaxation](#protein-structure-refinement-and-relaxation).

### Core 3D Geometric Data Structures and Operations
OpenFold utilizes a set of PyTorch-based data structures for efficient handling of 3D geometric operations, essential for representing and manipulating protein structures. These structures are designed to support batched tensor computations, allowing for parallel processing of multiple geometric entities.

The primary data structures are:
*   [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25): Represents 3D vectors, detailed in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py). This data structure supports standard vector arithmetic operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, along with dot products, cross products, and norm calculations. It provides a flexible way to manage single vectors or batches of vectors.
*   [`Rot3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py#L30): Represents 3x3 rotation matrices, detailed in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py). This structure facilitates operations such as matrix multiplication for composing rotations, inversion, and applying rotations to 3D points. It also supports conversions from and to quaternions and the construction of rotation matrices from two vectors, which is useful for defining coordinate frames.
*   [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30): Combines [`Rot3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py#L30) for rotation and [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25) for translation to represent 3D rigid transformations, detailed in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py). This allows for complex operations like transformation composition, inversion, and applying transformations to points. It also includes functionalities for converting to and from 4x4 homogeneous matrices, ensuring compatibility with various geometric computation frameworks.

These geometric data structures are housed in the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry) directory. The [`QuatRigid`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py#L10) module, found in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py), translates neural network activations into [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30) transformations using quaternion representations for rotation, providing a differentiable interface between model outputs and geometric transformations. Further details on this module can be found in [Quaternion-based Rigid Body Transformations](#protein-structure-representation-and-numerical-operations-quaternion-based-rigid-body-transformations). The [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/__init__.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/__init__.py) file aggregates these types and related utility functions, providing a centralized access point.

### Quaternion-based Rigid Body Transformations
The [`QuatRigid`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py#L10) module in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py) translates neural network activations into [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30) transformations, which are fundamental for representing and manipulating protein structures in 3D space. This module provides a differentiable interface, enabling the model to predict geometric changes directly from learned features.

The [`QuatRigid`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py#L10) class processes an input tensor of neural network activations. It uses a linear layer to transform these activations into a set of components that define a rotation and a translation. Rotations are represented using quaternions, which offer a compact and singularity-free method for describing 3D rotations, beneficial for neural network training due to their numerical stability. The module supports both full quaternion representation (four components) and a partial representation where the scalar component is implicitly set, providing flexibility in how rotations are encoded.

After extracting the quaternion components for rotation and a 3D vector for translation, the module constructs a [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30). This object combines the rotation and translation into a single, unified representation of a rigid body transformation. The use of [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30), [`Rot3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py#L30), and [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25) (as discussed in [Core 3D Geometric Data Structures and Operations](#protein-structure-representation-and-numerical-operations-core-3d-geometric-data-structures-and-operations)) encapsulates the underlying geometric operations, promoting modularity and maintainability of the codebase. This design choice also ensures that the geometric operations are consistent and mathematically sound across the OpenFold system.

## OpenFold Inference Examples
The [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/examples`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/examples) directory provides practical demonstrations of how to perform protein structure prediction inference using OpenFold. These examples guide users through the process of setting up and executing predictions, particularly for monomeric proteins, leveraging pre-trained models, and utilizing precomputed alignments to streamline the workflow.

A core example is the script for running monomeric protein inference located at [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/examples/monomer/inference.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/examples/monomer/inference.sh). This script showcases how to configure and execute the OpenFold model for single-chain proteins. It specifies the use of a pre-trained model configuration, targets a specific GPU device for computation, and sets a random seed to ensure reproducibility of results. A key feature highlighted is the option to use precomputed alignments, which can significantly accelerate the inference process by bypassing the computationally intensive alignment generation step.

### Running Monomeric Protein Inference
OpenFold offers an example script that facilitates protein structure inference for single-chain proteins. This script, located at [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/examples/monomer/inference.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/examples/monomer/inference.sh), illustrates how to utilize a pretrained OpenFold model to predict the three-dimensional structure of a monomeric protein.

The script configures the inference process by setting several key parameters:
*   **Model Configuration**: It specifies a particular pretrained model architecture, such as the [`model_1_ptm`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/tests/config.py#L6) preset. This selection dictates the pre-trained weights and architectural settings employed for the prediction.
*   **Device Targeting**: The script directs the model to execute on a designated CUDA-enabled GPU, which enables accelerated computation.
*   **Reproducibility**: To ensure consistent outcomes, a random seed is set for data processing operations.
*   **Precomputed Alignments**: The script supports the use of precomputed Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs). By leveraging existing alignments, the inference process can bypass the time-intensive step of generating them, thereby expediting the prediction workflow. For details on how these alignments are generated, refer to [Advanced Alignment Generation and Processing](#openfold-management-scripts-advanced-alignment-generation-and-processing).

This example serves as a practical guide for users to understand the fundamental steps involved in executing OpenFold for monomeric protein structure prediction.

## Experimentation and Model Evaluation
The OpenFold framework includes a dedicated component within [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments) for evaluating protein structure prediction models. This framework facilitates the assessment of prediction accuracy by comparing generated protein structures (decoys) against known native structures. This involves processing input PDB files as templates for the OpenFold model, calculating structural similarity metrics, and systematically storing the experimental results.

At its core, the evaluation process leverages the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py) script to manage the workflow. This script orchestrates the generation of protein structure predictions using the OpenFold model, often employing existing decoy structures as templates. Following prediction, the script performs a comparative analysis of the predicted structures against native structures to quantify their accuracy.

A key aspect of this evaluation is the generation of features from protein data. When structural templates are not available, placeholder features are generated by [`empty_placeholder_template_features`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L123). If ESM1b embeddings are utilized, [`make_embedding_features`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L137) loads these from a specified directory. All these components are integrated by [`make_processed_feature_dict`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L155), which combines sequence, Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA), and template features to prepare the comprehensive feature dictionary required by OpenFold. The [`score_decoy`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L217) function is central to this process, as it prepares template features from a given decoy, executes the OpenFold model for prediction, and subsequently parses the results.

To quantify the similarity between predicted and native structures, the framework employs specific metrics. [`jnp_rmsd`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L89) calculates the Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD), a measure of the average distance between the atoms of superimposed proteins, utilizing the [`kabsch`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L90) algorithm for optimal alignment. For more advanced structural comparisons, [`compute_tmscore`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L303) integrates an external TM-score program to evaluate and parse the TM-score, which assesses the topological similarity of protein structures. The results of these evaluations, including predicted PDBs and various metrics, are organized and persistently stored in CSV files using [`write_results`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L332). This systematic storage also includes mechanisms to track [`finished_decoys`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L382) and [`finished_targets`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L390), enabling the resumption of interrupted evaluation runs.

### Workflow for Decoy Scoring and Evaluation
The evaluation of protein structure prediction models in OpenFold involves a workflow that scores protein decoys against native structures. This process is managed by the code in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments). This framework orchestrates the generation of OpenFold predictions, using either native structures or alternative decoy structures as templates, and then quantifies the accuracy of these predictions.

The evaluation process begins with processing a list of target proteins and their corresponding decoys. For each decoy, a [`Decoy`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L326) namedtuple stores relevant metadata such as the target name, decoy identifier, and file paths. This metadata is crucial for organizing and managing the various inputs and outputs throughout the evaluation.

When preparing templates for OpenFold, the [`score_decoy`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L217) function converts an input protein decoy, represented as a [`protein`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/np/protein.py#L45) object, into the specific features required by the OpenFold model. This conversion includes generating template atom positions, masks, and amino acid types. The process also offers options for feature engineering, such as masking sidechain atoms or adding C-beta atoms for glycines, which can influence how the model incorporates template information.

Once the template features are prepared, an OpenFold model, configured through [`make_model_runner`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L106), generates a protein structure prediction. The model can be run with various settings, such as the number of recycles, which determines how many times the model refines its prediction. After the prediction, [`parse_results`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L185) extracts key information from OpenFold's output, including the predicted unrelaxed protein structure, per-residue predicted lDDT (pLDDT) scores, and a predicted TM-score.

The final step involves comparing the OpenFold prediction against the native structure and the original decoy. Structural similarity metrics such as Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) and TM-score are calculated. The [`jnp_rmsd`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L89) function computes RMSD, while [`compute_tmscore`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L303) executes an external TM-score program to obtain TM-score values. The [`write_results`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L332) function then aggregates these metrics, saves the predicted PDB files, and appends all results to CSV files, ensuring persistence and traceability of the evaluation outcomes. For a broader understanding of how structural similarity metrics and external tools are integrated into this process, refer to [Structural Similarity Metrics and External Tool Integration](#experimentation-and-model-evaluation-structural-similarity-metrics-and-external-tool-integration). The overall framework also supports resuming interrupted runs by tracking finished decoys and targets, which contributes to the robustness of the evaluation pipeline.

### Structural Similarity Metrics and External Tool Integration
Protein structure prediction models are quantitatively evaluated using structural similarity metrics to compare predicted protein structures (decoys) against known native structures. Key metrics include Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) and TM-score.

RMSD quantifies the average distance between the backbone atoms of superimposed protein structures. The [`jnp_rmsd`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L89) function, found in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py), calculates this metric using the Kabsch algorithm, which optimally superimposes one structure onto another to minimize the atomic distances.

TM-score (Template Modeling score) is another metric that assesses the topological similarity between two protein structures, with a score between 0 and 1, where 1 indicates a perfect match. Unlike RMSD, TM-score is less sensitive to local structural variations and more indicative of overall fold similarity. The calculation of TM-score is integrated through an external program. The [`compute_tmscore`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L303) function in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py) executes an external [`TMscore`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L50) executable, parses its output, and performs validation checks on sequence length and common residues.

The overall workflow for evaluating models and utilizing these metrics is detailed in [Workflow for Decoy Scoring and Evaluation](#experimentation-and-model-evaluation-workflow-for-decoy-scoring-and-evaluation). The [`write_results`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L332) function within [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py) consolidates these calculated metrics, along with predicted PDBs, into CSV files for persistent storage and analysis.

### Results Management and Persistent Storage
Experimental results, including predicted PDBs and various evaluation metrics, are organized and persistently stored within the [`experiments`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/config.py#L608) directory. The evaluation script, found at [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py), manages the saving of predicted protein structures as PDB files and appends all collected evaluation metrics to CSV files. To ensure reproducibility and efficient processing, the system tracks [`finished_decoys`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L382) and [`finished_targets`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/experiments/test_templates_openfold.py#L390), enabling the resumption of interrupted runs without redundant computations. This persistent storage mechanism allows for comprehensive analysis of model performance and comparison across different experiments. For a deeper understanding of the evaluation process, refer to [Workflow for Decoy Scoring and Evaluation](#experimentation-and-model-evaluation-workflow-for-decoy-scoring-and-evaluation).

## Core Utility Functions and Performance Optimization
The [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils) directory provides a collection of functions designed to support and enhance the OpenFold system, covering various aspects of protein structure prediction, numerical operations, and performance optimization.

For handling protein structures, the system includes methods for converting between [`atom14`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/feats.py#L56) and [`atom37`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L798) representations, computing rigid body frames, and generating atomic positions from torsion angles, as detailed in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/all_atom_multimer.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/all_atom_multimer.py). These functions are essential for managing different granularities of atomic data and coordinate systems. Further, general feature generation for models, such as pseudo-beta atom coordinates, template features, and distance matrix calculations, is handled in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/feats.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/feats.py). The [`Rigid`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/rigid_utils.py#L813) class, defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/rigid_utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/rigid_utils.py), enables operations for batched 3D rotations and rigid transformations, supporting both matrix and quaternion representations. This class underpins many of the geometric transformations within the system, including composition, inversion, and point application. The system also supports advanced multi-chain handling, with [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py) addressing arbitrary chain ordering in multimer predictions by finding optimal permutations and transformations to minimize RMSD. The structural superimposition technique is also supported in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/superimposition.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/superimposition.py).

A suite of loss functions crucial for model training is implemented in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py). This includes structural losses like Frame Aligned Point Error (FAPE), lDDT for local structural similarity, distogram losses for residue-residue distances, and violation losses for penalizing steric clashes and bond geometry deviations. This file also addresses the complexities of symmetric atoms by implementing renaming strategies to ensure consistent error calculation. The system also includes [`AlphaFoldLRScheduler`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/lr_schedulers.py#L4) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/lr_schedulers.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/lr_schedulers.py), which implements a learning rate schedule with linear warmup, a plateau phase, and exponential decay, mirroring the AlphaFold 2 training regimen.

Performance optimization is a key focus, with several strategies implemented to handle large models and sequences. Activation checkpointing, managed by [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/checkpointing.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/checkpointing.py), dynamically selects between PyTorch and DeepSpeed implementations to trade computation time for memory usage. The chunking of large tensors, facilitated by [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py), processes inputs in smaller, manageable parts to mitigate memory constraints, and can dynamically tune optimal chunk sizes. For improved inference performance, OpenFold integrates NVIDIA TensorRT, as detailed in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_lazy_compiler.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_lazy_compiler.py) and [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_utils.py), enabling lazy compilation, persistent engine management, and dynamic input shapes. Mixed-precision training support, provided by [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/precision_utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/precision_utils.py), automates the casting of tensors between [`float32`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/tests/data_utils.py#L44), [`bfloat16`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/build_deepspeed_config.py#L275), and [`float16`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/model/primitives.py#L52). Furthermore, the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel) directory contains custom CUDA kernels for optimized attention operations, particularly for in-place softmax within [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/attention_core.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/attention_core.py), providing significant performance gains.

For structural calculations, core data structures for 3D geometry are provided in the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry) directory. This includes [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25) for vectors, [`Rot3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py#L30) for rotation matrices, and [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30) for rigid transformations, all built on PyTorch tensors for efficient, batched operations. These structures support various arithmetic and transformation operations. The [`QuatRigid`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py#L10) module in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py) translates neural network activations into [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30) transformations using quaternion representations for rotation, providing a differentiable interface between model outputs and geometric transformations.

Other utilities include mechanisms for importing pre-trained model weights, handling transformations between different weight formats (e.g., JAX NPZ to PyTorch [`state_dict`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/lr_schedulers.py#L54)), and managing compatibility with older OpenFold model versions, as seen in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/import_weights.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/import_weights.py). Performance logging and evaluation are handled by [`PerformanceLoggingCallback`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/logger.py#L29) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/logger.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/logger.py), which measures and logs metrics like throughput and latency during training and testing.

### Core Geometric Data Structures and Rigid Transformations
OpenFold utilizes a suite of PyTorch-based data structures for efficient and batched handling of 3D geometric information, which is fundamental for protein structure representation and manipulation. This includes specialized classes for 3D vectors, rotation matrices, and rigid transformations, enabling advanced operations essential for protein modeling.

The primary geometric data structures are:
*   [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25): Represents 3D vectors. This class allows for standard vector arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), dot and cross products, and calculates vector norms. It supports both single vectors and batches of vectors, facilitating vectorized computations crucial for neural network processing. The module also provides utilities for calculating [`square_euclidean_distance`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L174), [`euclidean_distance`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L214), and [`dihedral_angle`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L236) between [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25) instances in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py).
*   [`Rot3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py#L30): Encapsulates 3x3 rotation matrices. This structure supports matrix multiplication for composing rotations, inversion to find the opposite rotation, and applying rotations to 3D points. It can be constructed from two vectors to define an orthonormal basis, or from quaternions, allowing for flexible representation of 3D rotations in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py).
*   [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30): Combines a [`Rot3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rotation_matrix.py#L30) and a [`Vec3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L25) to represent complete 3D rigid transformations, which include both rotation and translation. This class enables transformation composition, inversion, and applying rigid transformations to 3D points. It also supports conversion to and from 4x4 homogeneous matrices, ensuring compatibility with various geometric frameworks in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py).

These foundational data structures, collectively exposed via [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/__init__.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/__init__.py), provide a robust framework for managing and operating on 3D coordinates and orientations within OpenFold. For instance, the [`QuatRigid`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py#L10) module in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/quat_rigid.py) translates neural network activations into [`Rigid3Array`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/rigid_matrix_vector.py#L30) transformations using quaternion representations for rotation, providing a differentiable interface between model outputs and geometric transformations. This suite of tools underpins the model's ability to iteratively refine and predict protein structures in 3D space. More information on geometric operations and rigid body transformations can be found in [Geometric Operations and Rigid Body Transformations](#protein-structure-prediction-core-geometric-operations-and-rigid-body-transformations).

### Optimization with Custom CUDA Kernels for Attention
OpenFold incorporates custom PyTorch autograd functions and CUDA kernels to optimize attention operations, particularly focusing on in-place softmax calculations for enhanced performance. This approach leverages manual implementation of the forward and backward passes, which is key for integrating custom C++/CUDA kernels and tailoring gradient computations.

The core attention mechanism is handled by [`AttentionCoreFunction`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/attention_core.py#L26) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/attention_core.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/attention_core.py), a [`torch.autograd.Function`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/attention_core.py#L26) subclass. This function computes initial attention logits, applies optional bias tensors, and then uses a custom CUDA kernel for an in-place modification of these logits. The final output is then computed, and the necessary tensors are saved for the backward pass. The [`backward`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/attention_core.py#L62) method meticulously calculates gradients for all inputs, utilizing a dedicated CUDA kernel for the in-place operation's gradient computation. This custom autograd function allows for direct integration of highly optimized GPU code, bypassing potential overheads of standard PyTorch operations.

The CUDA kernels themselves are defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda_kernel.cu`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda_kernel.cu). These kernels implement an in-place softmax operation and its gradient, specifically optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. They employ warp-level optimizations, such as [`WarpAllReduceMax`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda_kernel.cu#L33) and [`WarpAllReduceSum`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda_kernel.cu#L40), for efficient reductions within warps. The kernels support both [`float`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/geometry/vector.py#L22) and [`at::BFloat16`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda_kernel.cu#L124) data types, ensuring compatibility with mixed-precision training. Host-side wrappers in the same file launch these kernels after validating inputs and dispatching based on data types. The C++ interface in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda.cpp`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda.cpp) exposes these CUDA functions to Python, making them accessible as [`forward_`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda.cpp#L35) and [`backward_`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda.cpp#L40) methods. For non-CUDA environments, [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda_stub.cpp`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/softmax_cuda_stub.cpp) provides placeholder stubs that raise errors if called, indicating the GPU-specific nature of these optimizations. Compatibility across different PyTorch versions is maintained through macros defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/compat.h`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/kernel/csrc/compat.h). The decision to use in-place operations and warp-level parallelism is a deliberate design choice aimed at reducing memory allocations, minimizing data transfers, and maximizing computational efficiency on GPU architectures.

### Multi-chain Permutation Alignment and Superimposition
Multi-chain protein predictions present a unique challenge due to the arbitrary ordering of chains in both predicted and ground truth structures. To accurately evaluate or utilize multi-chain predictions, it is necessary to align the predicted chains to their corresponding ground truth chains, minimizing the Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD). This process involves identifying the optimal permutation of predicted chains to match ground truth chains and then applying a rigid body transformation to superimpose them.

The system addresses this by first parsing and organizing ground truth features by individual chains, often referred to as asymmetric units. An "anchor" chain, typically the least asymmetric or longest chain, is selected to provide a robust starting point for alignment. The core of the alignment process relies on the Kabsch algorithm, implemented in functions such as [`kabsch_rotation`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py#L35) within [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py), which calculates the optimal rotation and translation to superimpose two sets of 3D points.

Following the initial anchoring, a greedy alignment approach is employed. This method iteratively matches predicted chains to ground truth chains by finding the pairing that minimizes RMSD. This iterative process ensures that the best possible match is found across all chains, accounting for potential misordering in the model's output. The [`greedy_align`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py#L167) function in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/multi_chain_permutation.py) implements this strategy. Once the optimal permutation is determined, ground truth features are reordered, and padding is applied to ensure consistent tensor dimensions for downstream calculations, such as loss computation.

The structural superimposition itself can be performed on both NumPy arrays and batched PyTorch tensors, as seen in the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/superimposition.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/superimposition.py) module. This module provides functions that perform RMSD-minimizing structural superimposition of atomic coordinates using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). It is capable of handling masks, allowing specific atoms to be included or excluded from the superimposition calculation. For batched operations, the system efficiently processes each sample independently, extracting unmasked coordinates, superimposing them using the Kabsch algorithm (via [`_superimpose_single`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/superimposition.py#L37) calling into [`_superimpose_np`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/superimposition.py#L19)), and then reconstructing the full-sized superimposed coordinates. This approach ensures that the model can accurately evaluate predictions against native structures, even when dealing with complex multi-chain protein assemblies.

### Advanced Loss Functions for Structure Prediction
The core of OpenFold's training mechanism relies on a sophisticated collection of loss functions, primarily managed by the [`AlphaFoldLoss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1685) class within [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py). This class aggregates various individual loss components, each designed to penalize specific types of discrepancies between predicted protein structures and their ground truth. The selection and weighting of these losses are configurable, allowing for flexible optimization strategies.

One fundamental loss is the Frame Aligned Point Error (FAPE), implemented by [`compute_fape`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L82) and applied through [`backbone_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L169) and [`sidechain_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L235). FAPE measures the distance between predicted and true atomic positions within local coordinate frames, which is crucial for accurately positioning amino acid residues and their side chains. This loss is sensitive to both positional and orientational errors of the rigid bodies that constitute the protein structure.

To ensure physical realism, OpenFold employs several structural violation losses. These include [`between_residue_bond_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L782), [`between_residue_clash_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L942), and [`within_residue_violations`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1096), all part of the [`find_structural_violations`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1186) function. These functions penalize deviations from ideal bond lengths and angles, as well as steric clashes between atoms, contributing to the overall [`violation_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1432). This encourages the model to generate physically plausible protein geometries.

Accuracy of predicted residue-residue distances is evaluated using the [`distogram_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L562), which compares the model's predicted distance distributions to binned true distances using cross-entropy. Similarly, the [`lddt_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L507) and [`tm_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L721) assess structural similarity. The [`lddt_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L507) uses the Local Distance Difference Test (lDDT) score, a metric for local structural similarity, while [`tm_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L721) is based on the TM-score, which evaluates overall topological similarity. These losses provide a robust measure of how well the predicted structure matches the ground truth at both local and global scales.

A unique aspect of the loss system is its handling of symmetric amino acid side chains (e.g., Valine, Leucine). The [`compute_renamed_ground_truth`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1463) function from AlphaFold's Algorithm 26 addresses this by finding the optimal permutation of symmetric atoms in the ground truth that minimizes error against the prediction. This ensures that the model is not unfairly penalized for predicting a biologically equivalent, yet atomically permuted, configuration.

Additionally, OpenFold utilizes a [`masked_msa_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1595), which is a self-supervised task similar to masked language modeling. This loss encourages the model to accurately predict masked amino acids in the Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA), thereby improving its understanding of sequence context. For multimeric proteins, the [`chain_center_of_mass_loss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1628) specifically penalizes errors in the relative positioning of different protein chains, guiding the model to predict correct quaternary structures.

The overall [`AlphaFoldLoss`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/loss.py#L1685) function aggregates these various components, scaling each by a configurable weight. This modular and configurable approach allows for fine-tuning the training process to prioritize different aspects of protein structure prediction, from atomic accuracy to global topology and multimer interactions.

### Performance Acceleration with TensorRT Integration
OpenFold integrates NVIDIA TensorRT to optimize the inference performance of its protein structure prediction models. This integration is managed through a system that compiles and executes models or submodules using TensorRT engines, with various configurations for precision and dynamic input handling.

The core mechanism involves [`TrtCompiler`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_lazy_compiler.py#L382) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_lazy_compiler.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_lazy_compiler.py), which wraps a PyTorch neural network module and replaces its forward pass with a TensorRT-accelerated version. This allows for lazy compilation, where the TensorRT engine is built and saved only when it's first required. Once compiled, these engines are serialized and persisted to disk as [`.plan`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/run_pretrained_openfold.py#L509) files, eliminating the need for recompilation in subsequent runs. This persistent storage significantly reduces startup overhead.

The system supports dynamic input shapes, which is crucial for handling variable-length protein sequences in models like AlphaFold. Input profiles can be defined to specify minimum, optimal, and maximum input dimensions, enabling TensorRT to generate engines capable of efficiently processing a range of sequence lengths. The [`instrument_with_trt_compile`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_utils.py#L27) function in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/tensorrt_utils.py) specifically configures the [`evoformer`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/config.py#L1010) component of the OpenFold model for TensorRT compilation, defining dynamic shapes for sequence length and generating these input profiles.

The integration also includes a fallback mechanism: if TensorRT inference encounters an issue, such as a shape mismatch outside the defined profiles, the system can revert to using the original PyTorch forward method. This ensures robustness and continued functionality even under unexpected input conditions. Additionally, the framework allows for targeting specific submodules for TensorRT compilation, enabling fine-grained optimization. For more details on the core geometric structures used within OpenFold, refer to [Core Geometric Data Structures and Rigid Transformations](#core-utility-functions-and-performance-optimization-core-geometric-data-structures-and-rigid-transformations).

### Efficient Memory Management: Checkpointing and Chunking
To address memory constraints when training large models, OpenFold employs activation checkpointing and chunking. Activation checkpointing, managed by [`get_checkpoint_fn`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/checkpointing.py#L29) and [`checkpoint_blocks`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/checkpointing.py#L43) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/checkpointing.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/checkpointing.py), allows for a trade-off between computation and memory by not storing intermediate activations during the forward pass. These activations are recomputed during the backward pass, reducing the overall memory footprint. The implementation dynamically selects between PyTorch's native checkpointing and DeepSpeed's optimized version, integrating with DeepSpeed for distributed training and memory optimization when available.

Chunking, facilitated by the utilities in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py), enables processing large tensors in smaller, manageable portions. The [`chunk_layer`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py#L213) function applies a given neural network layer to inputs chunk by chunk, which is essential when the full input would exceed available GPU memory. This process involves splitting inputs, applying the layer, and reassembling the outputs. For scenarios with very large tensors, [`_chunk_slice`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py#L177) and [`_get_minimal_slice_set`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py#L59) are used to extract chunks efficiently without memory-intensive full tensor reshapes. Additionally, the [`ChunkSizeTuner`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/utils/chunk_utils.py#L345) class dynamically determines an optimal [`chunk_size`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/config.py#L318) by iteratively testing different sizes to find the largest size that avoids out-of-memory errors, caching this value for consistent input shapes. This systematic approach to memory management allows OpenFold to handle substantial protein data and complex model architectures within typical hardware constraints.

## Bioinformatics Tool Wrappers
The directory [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools) provides Python wrappers for integrating various external bioinformatics command-line tools into OpenFold's protein sequence analysis pipeline. These wrappers abstract the complexities of executing external binaries, managing temporary files, and parsing their diverse outputs, enabling the system to generate crucial features like Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) and template information.

The wrappers facilitate the use of tools such as HHblits for iterative sequence database searches, HHsearch for HMM-profile-based database searches, hmmbuild for constructing Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) from MSAs, hmmsearch for querying databases with HMMs, jackhmmer for iterative sequence searches, and Kalign for performing multiple sequence alignments. Each wrapper, like the [`HHBlits`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hhblits.py#L30) class in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hhblits.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hhblits.py) or the [`Jackhmmer`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py#L30) class in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py), handles the specific command-line arguments, input/output formats, and error conditions of its respective tool. They typically employ [`subprocess.Popen`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/kalign.py#L93) for binary execution and utilize [`utils.tmpdir_manager`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/kalign.py#L75) from [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/utils.py) to manage temporary files, ensuring a clean and controlled execution environment.

A key aspect of these wrappers is their ability to parse the output of these tools. For example, [`HHSearch`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hhsearch.py#L27) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hhsearch.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hhsearch.py) parses HHR outputs into structured [`TemplateHit`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L57) objects. Similarly, [`hmmsearch`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hmmsearch.py#L27) in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hmmsearch.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hmmsearch.py) processes Stockholm-formatted output. The module [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/parse_msa_files.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/parse_msa_files.py) further supports this by providing utilities for parsing multiple MSA files (in Stockholm or A3M formats) in parallel, enhancing efficiency when preparing large datasets. For more details on how these features are integrated into the overall data processing pipeline, refer to [Data Processing and Feature Generation Pipeline](#protein-structure-prediction-core-data-processing-and-feature-generation-pipeline). The handling of [`parsers.TemplateHit`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/templates.py#L111) objects is further detailed in [Template Feature Extraction and Processing](#protein-data-handling-and-preprocessing-template-feature-extraction-and-processing).

### Execution and Temporary File Management
OpenFold integrates external bioinformatics tools by wrapping their command-line binaries in Python classes. This approach involves executing these external programs as subprocesses, managing their input and output, and handling temporary files to ensure efficient and clean operation.

For example, tools like [`HHblits`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/docs/source/index.md#L51), [`HHsearch`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/docs/source/original_readme.md#L390), [`hmmbuild`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hmmbuild.py#L25), [`hmmsearch`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/hmmsearch.py#L27), [`jackhmmer`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py#L30), and [`Kalign`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/kalign.py#L36) are invoked using [`subprocess.Popen`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/kalign.py#L93) in their respective wrapper classes within the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools) directory. These wrappers construct the necessary command-line arguments based on method parameters, pass input data (often via temporary files), and capture the standard output and error streams. This allows for programmatic control over these tools and facilitates error handling by checking process return codes and logging diagnostics.

A key aspect of this integration is the systematic management of temporary files and directories. A [`tmpdir_manager`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/utils.py#L27) context manager, defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/utils.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/utils.py), is widely used across these wrappers. This manager creates a temporary directory for each tool execution, writes input files to it, directs tool output to files within it, and ensures that the entire directory is automatically cleaned up once the operation is complete, even if errors occur. This design prevents accumulation of intermediate files and maintains a clean filesystem.

Some tools also feature advanced handling for large datasets. For instance, the [`Jackhmmer`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py#L30) wrapper in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py) can stream large database chunks, downloading them concurrently and processing them sequentially to manage memory and disk usage effectively. This minimizes I/O wait times and enables the system to work with databases that might otherwise be too large to fit in local storage. Parsing the diverse output formats from these tools (e.g., A3M, Stockholm, HHR) is handled separately; see [Parsing Tool Outputs and MSA File Handling](#bioinformatics-tool-wrappers-parsing-tool-outputs-and-msa-file-handling).

### Parsing Tool Outputs and MSA File Handling
OpenFold includes utilities for parsing various bioinformatics output formats, such as FASTA, Stockholm, A3M, and HHR, which are crucial for processing sequence alignments and template search results. These parsing functions convert raw text outputs from tools like HHblits, Jackhmmer, and HMMsearch into structured Python objects for further processing.

The [`Msa`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L29) dataclass, defined in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py), represents multiple sequence alignments, storing sequences, deletion matrices, and descriptions. It provides methods for validation and truncation. Similarly, the [`TemplateHit`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L57) dataclass in the same file structures information about hits from template searches, including alignment details and residue indices.

Specific parsing functions handle different formats:
*   [`parse_fasta`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L70) processes FASTA strings into sequences and descriptions.
*   [`parse_stockholm`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L101) and [`parse_a3m`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L163) convert Stockholm and A3M formatted MSAs into [`Msa`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L29) objects, calculating deletion matrices and handling insertions. Utilities like [`convert_stockholm_to_a3m`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L211) and [`truncate_stockholm_msa`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L293) facilitate format conversion and size management of MSAs.
*   [`parse_hhr`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L519) processes HHR files from tools like HHsearch and HHblits into a list of [`TemplateHit`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L57) objects, extracting aligned sequences and residue indices.
*   [`parse_e_values_from_tblout`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L539) extracts E-values from Jackhmmer's tabular output.
*   [`parse_hmmsearch_a3m`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L603) and [`parse_hmmsearch_sto`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L649) parse HMMsearch outputs, extracting [`TemplateHit`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/parsers.py#L57) objects and associated metadata like PDB IDs and chain information.

For efficiency, the system supports parallel parsing of multiple MSA files. The [`run_parse_all_msa_files_multiprocessing`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/parse_msa_files.py#L24) function in [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/parse_msa_files.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/openfold/data/tools/parse_msa_files.py) uses a process pool to concurrently parse Stockholm and A3M files from a specified directory, collecting the results and handling any parsing errors. This allows for faster data preparation when dealing with large datasets of alignment files. The [`main`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/train_openfold.py#L284) function in the same file orchestrates this parallel parsing and serializes the processed MSA data into a pickle file for persistent storage and subsequent use.

The various bioinformatics tool wrappers, as described in [Bioinformatics Tool Wrappers](#bioinformatics-tool-wrappers), rely on these parsing utilities to interpret the output of external binaries and integrate the information into OpenFold's data processing pipeline.

## OpenFold Management Scripts
The [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts) directory centralizes a collection of utilities for managing the OpenFold environment and its various workflows. These scripts facilitate tasks such as setting up the development environment, downloading necessary biological databases, generating protein sequence alignments, configuring DeepSpeed for optimized training and inference, and converting model checkpoints.

Environment setup and the installation of third-party dependencies are handled by scripts like [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/activate_conda_env.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/activate_conda_env.sh), [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/deactivate_conda_env.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/deactivate_conda_env.sh), and [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/install_third_party_dependencies.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/install_third_party_dependencies.sh). These scripts ensure the Conda environment is properly configured and essential bioinformatics tools, such as HH-suite, along with performance libraries like CUTLASS, are installed.

A comprehensive suite of scripts is dedicated to downloading and preparing various biological databases. This includes [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_alphafold_dbs.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_alphafold_dbs.sh), which orchestrates the download of multiple AlphaFold-related databases (BFD, MGnify, PDB70, PDB mmCIF, Uniref30, Uniref90, UniProt, PDB SeqRes) by invoking specialized sub-scripts. Model parameters for both AlphaFold and OpenFold are downloaded via [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_alphafold_params.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_alphafold_params.sh) and [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_openfold_params.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_openfold_params.sh) respectively. These scripts manage the acquisition of pre-trained weights and other essential data for model operation. Specific scripts such as [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_cameo.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/download_cameo.py) also handle the acquisition of CAMEO protein data, including CIF files and FASTA sequences.

For generating protein sequence alignments, scripts like [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/precompute_alignments.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/precompute_alignments.py) and [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/precompute_alignments_mmseqs.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/precompute_alignments_mmseqs.py) are used. These orchestrate the execution of tools like JackHMMER, HHblits, HMMsearch, and MMseqs2 to create multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and template information, which are crucial features for protein structure prediction. The output of these processes can then be converted to a FASTA format using [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_data_to_fasta.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_data_to_fasta.py). For large-scale alignment generation, especially on HPC clusters, the specialized script [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/slurm_scripts/run_uniclust30_search.sh`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/slurm_scripts/run_uniclust30_search.sh) facilitates Uniclust30 all-against-all alignments within a SLURM environment, managing data transfer, input splitting, and parallel execution.

The management of these alignment databases is further supported by scripts in the [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_db_scripts`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_db_scripts) directory. These scripts, including [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_db_scripts/create_alignment_db.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_db_scripts/create_alignment_db.py) and [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_db_scripts/create_alignment_db_sharded.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/alignment_db_scripts/create_alignment_db_sharded.py), are responsible for creating, extending, and consolidating protein alignment databases. This includes handling sharding for performance and efficiently integrating non-unique protein chains, as described in [Protein Alignment Database Management](#openfold-management-scripts-protein-alignment-database-management).

DeepSpeed integration is managed through scripts such as [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/build_deepspeed_config.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/build_deepspeed_config.py), which dynamically generates DeepSpeed configuration JSON files, and [`/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/deepspeed_inference_test.py`](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold/scripts/deepspeed_inference_test.py), designed for testing DeepSpeed's inference capabilities.
